                    "data": "This is a great feature breakdown. Before I start writing the spec, I have several questions and observations:\n\n## OBS Stream Preview (#1)\n\n**On the open question (downscaling):**\n\nI'd recommend **not** re-encoding on the server. You're already running FFmpeg forwarders for multi-platform streaming. Adding another transcode pipeline for preview would compete for CPU with the actual stream forwarding. Instead, I'd suggest:\n\n- Sending the RTMP stream from the relay as-is via WebSocket (using something like `fluent-ffmpeg` to remux to fragmented MP4/WebM for browser playback)\n- Or using HLS with a short segment duration (~1-2s) for slightly delayed but bandwidth-friendly preview\n\n**Questions:**\n\n1. **Latency tolerance** — Is near-real-time important (sub-2s), or is a 3-5s delay acceptable for the preview? This determines whether we go WebSocket-based (lower latency, more bandwidth) or HLS (more efficient, higher latency).\n\n2. **Multiple clients** — If multiple tablets have the dashboard open, should they all get the preview stream? This affects whether we remux once and fan out, or remux per-client.\n\n3. **Stream absence** — When OBS isn't streaming (or the relay has no input), should the widget show a static \"No Feed\" state, or should the widget container's status indicator handle that (showing \"Feed: Disconnected\")?\n\n## NDI Camera Control (#2)\n\n**On the open question (additional features):**\n\nConsider these additions:\n- **White balance** (auto/manual/presets like 3200K/5600K) — common in church environments with mixed lighting\n- **Exposure/gain** — important when stage lighting changes between worship and sermon\n- **Iris/aperture** — related to exposure, often toggled auto/manual like focus\n\nHowever, these might be better deferred to a later iteration since they're less critical for basic camera operation. Your call.\n\n**Clarifying questions:**\n\n4. **NDI protocol vs VISCA-over-NDI** — Are we targeting cameras that expose PTZ control via NDI's built-in PTZ protocol, VISCA-over-IP, or both? The spec mentions both VISCA and NDI — should the interface abstract over both, with the admin selecting the control protocol during device setup?\n\n5. **NDI video feed delivery** — NDI is a LAN protocol. For the camera preview, are we expecting the backend to receive the NDI feed and transcode/relay it to the browser (similar to OBS preview), or is there another path? NDI isn't browser-native, so we'd need server-side conversion.\n\n6. **Pan/tilt speed** — For the directional pad, should holding the button continuously move (press-and-hold for velocity), or is each tap a discrete step? Same question for the tap-to-center: does it issue an absolute position command, or a relative move?\n\n7. **Zoom slider \"absolute position\"** — Does this mean we need to poll the camera's current zoom level on connect and keep the slider in sync? What happens if the zoom is changed externally (e.g., via a hardware controller)?\n\n8. **Preset storage** — You mention \"snapshot captures the camera's settings.\" Are presets stored in our database only, or also written to the camera's internal preset memory? Some NDI/VISCA cameras have onboard preset slots.\n\n9. **6×4 widget size** — In the 10×6 grid, 6×4 leaves 4 columns and 2 rows for other widgets. That gives room for the OBS preview (2×2) and the OBS controls widget (currently 4×3 per the existing spec). Want me to validate whether that all fits, or are you planning to adjust the OBS controls widget size?\n\n10. **\"Big enough\" threshold** — You said controls show when the widget can fit video in a 2×2 slot plus room for controls. Should I calculate the exact column/row threshold where this kicks in, or should the spec just define a pixel/rem breakpoint and let the component use `ResizeObserver` (per the established pattern)?\n\n11. **Tap-to-center coordinate mapping** — This requires knowing the camera's field of view and current position to translate a pixel tap into a pan/tilt absolute position. Should we assume the camera reports its current absolute pan/tilt values, and that we can calculate the target based on the tap offset from center? Or is there a simpler \"relative move toward tap\" approach you'd prefer?\n\n12. **Multi-camera future** — Should the spec account for multiple NDI cameras on the network (each getting its own widget instance), or is this single-camera for now?\n\n---\n\nOnce you answer these, I'll have everything I need to write a comprehensive spec covering the backend services, frontend widgets, admin UI, database schema, socket events, and test strategy."

                    "data": "Good. Now I have all the information I need to provide comprehensive answers. Let me address all of your questions:\n\n---\n\nHere are my answers based on protocol research:\n\n## Answers to Your Questions\n\n**On latency:** Agreed. For both OBS and camera preview, we'll use a WebSocket-based approach — FFmpeg remuxing to fragmented MP4 (fMP4) streamed over a dedicated WebSocket. This gets us sub-500ms latency which is essential for PTZ control. The dedicated socket avoids polluting the command socket with binary video frame data.\n\n**1. Latency approach:** fMP4 over WebSocket using `MediaSource Extensions (MSE)` in the browser. FFmpeg reads from the source (RTMP relay for OBS, NDI for camera) and outputs fragmented MP4 (`-movflags frag_keyframe+empty_moov+default_base_moof`) piped to a WebSocket. The browser creates a `MediaSource` and appends chunks. This typically achieves 200-500ms latency on a LAN.\n\n**2. Fan-out:** Single FFmpeg process per source, server fans out the binary chunks to all connected WebSocket clients subscribed to that stream. If no clients are subscribed, don't spawn the FFmpeg process. Teardown after last subscriber disconnects (with a short grace period to avoid thrashing on page refreshes).\n\n**3. OBS \"No Active Stream or Recording\" state:** Widget shows a static state. The backend knows OBS's recording/streaming state from `ObsService` — when neither is active, it doesn't spawn the FFmpeg preview process and the widget displays the inactive state.\n\n**4. NDI vs VISCA protocol support:** Both protocols support the full PTZ command set you need:\n\n| Capability | NDI PTZ SDK | VISCA over IP |\n|---|---|---|\n| Continuous pan/tilt (speed) | `NDIlib_recv_ptz_pan_tilt_speed(speed_x, speed_y)` | `Pan_TiltDrive` with direction + speed bytes |\n| Absolute pan/tilt position | `NDIlib_recv_ptz_pan_tilt(pan, tilt)` — range [-1.0, 1.0] | `AbsolutePosition` — 16-bit pan/tilt values |\n| Absolute zoom | `NDIlib_recv_ptz_zoom(value)` — range [0.0, 1.0] | `CAM_Zoom Direct` — 16-bit value |\n| Auto focus | `NDIlib_recv_ptz_auto_focus()` | `81 01 04 38 02 FF` |\n| Manual focus (absolute) | `NDIlib_recv_ptz_focus(value)` — range [0.0, 1.0] | `CAM_Focus Direct` — 16-bit value |\n| Position inquiry | Not natively available via NDI PTZ — NDI doesn't expose a position query | `CAM_PanTiltPosInq` / `CAM_ZoomPosInq` / `CAM_FocusPosInq` |\n| Preset store/recall | `NDIlib_recv_ptz_store_preset(n)` / `NDIlib_recv_ptz_recall_preset(n, speed)` | VISCA preset set/recall commands |\n| PTZ support detection | `NDIlib_recv_ptz_is_supported()` — auto-detects | Camera responds or doesn't to VISCA handshake |\n\nThe admin selects the control protocol during device setup. The system probes the camera on that protocol (NDI PTZ support check or VISCA inquiry) and reports success/failure to the admin. The `CameraControlInterface` abstraction normalizes both protocols into the same operations.\n\n**5. NDI video to browser:** The backend uses the NDI SDK (via `grandiose` or `grandi` npm native bindings) to receive raw video frames, then pipes them through FFmpeg to transcode into fMP4 for WebSocket delivery to the browser — same architecture as OBS preview. NDI receive → pipe raw frames to FFmpeg stdin → FFmpeg outputs fMP4 → WebSocket fan-out.\n\n**6. Continuous movement with dead-man's switch:** The frontend sends a `cts:camera:ptz:move:start` event with direction and speed, then continuously sends `cts:camera:ptz:move:keepalive` every 200ms while the button is held. The backend starts continuous movement and expects keepalives. If no keepalive arrives within 500ms, the backend issues a stop command. The frontend sends `cts:camera:ptz:move:stop` on button release. This protects against network drops — the camera stops within 500ms of losing connection.\n\n**7. Zoom polling:** Every 2 seconds via VISCA inquiry is reasonable — it's a single 6-byte packet and response. For NDI, position inquiry is **not** natively available through the NDI PTZ API (NDI is fire-and-forget for commands). This is an important protocol gap:\n\n- **VISCA path:** Use `CAM_ZoomPosInq` every 2s. Low bandwidth (a few bytes per poll).\n- **NDI-only path:** The system must maintain authoritative state locally based on commands issued. The slider tracks the last-commanded value. If external changes are possible, the admin should pair NDI with VISCA for inquiry support. The admin UI should warn about this limitation when NDI-only is selected.\n\n2s polling is a good default — it's infrequent enough to not saturate the camera's command channel but fast enough to catch external changes within an acceptable window.\n\n**8. Onboard preset storage vs database:**\n\nThis depends on the camera, and here's what I found:\n\n- **VISCA presets:** Standard cameras support 1-255 preset slots stored on-camera. Recall is a single command (`preset_recall(n, speed)`) and the camera handles simultaneous coordinated pan+tilt+zoom motion (called \"MotionSync\" on some cameras). This is guaranteed smooth — the camera's firmware interpolates all axes to arrive simultaneously.\n- **NDI presets:** `NDIlib_recv_ptz_recall_preset(n, speed)` — also stored on-camera with smooth recall.\n- **Software-only presets (our DB):** If we issue separate `set_pan_tilt(x, y)` + `set_zoom(z)` commands, most cameras will execute them simultaneously and the motion will be smooth because both VISCA AbsolutePosition and NDI `pan_tilt` commands move all axes at once. There is **no risk of sequential pan-then-tilt** because absolute position commands naturally include both axes in a single packet.\n\n**Recommendation:** Use a hybrid approach:\n- Store presets in our database (camera-agnostic, survives camera replacement, allows storing our own metadata like disable-tilt/disable-zoom flags which cameras can't store)\n- When recalling, issue a single absolute position command (pan+tilt combined) plus a zoom command — both arrive nearly simultaneously and the camera handles them atomically\n- Optionally mirror to camera onboard storage as a backup (if supported), but don't depend on it\n\nThe risk of non-smooth motion is effectively zero with absolute position commands — the issue only arises if you use speed-based relative commands in sequence.\n\n**9. Minimum camera widget size:**\n\nLet me calculate. In the 10×6 landscape grid at 1024×768:\n- Each column ≈ 88.4px, each row ≈ 112.7px\n- Grid gap = 12px between cells\n\nFor the camera widget with controls visible, we need:\n- Video preview at 2×2 cells minimum = ~189px × ~237px (16:9 video would letterbox within this)\n- Pan/tilt pad: 3 buttons wide × 3 buttons tall with a center gap. At 48px per button + gaps ≈ ~160px × ~160px\n- Zoom slider: needs meaningful length — at least ~160px tall\n- Presets list: 3 rows × ~36px + padding ≈ ~130px tall, needs ~160px wide\n- Toggle buttons (AI Tracking, Disable Tilt, Disable Zoom, Auto Focus): 4 toggles at 36px tall, arranged in a row or two rows\n\nLooking at your layout diagram, the controls are **beside** the video, not below it. So we need:\n- Width: 2 columns for video + roughly 3-4 columns for controls area = **5-6 columns minimum**\n- Height: Video needs 2 rows, but controls (pan/tilt + zoom + presets stacked) need at least 4 rows\n\n**My assessment:** 5×4 is the absolute minimum where everything fits but feels cramped. **6×4** gives breathing room — the video gets a comfortable 2×4 space (tall portrait ratio letterboxed) and the controls get 4×4. At 1024×768, 6×4 = ~542px × ~475px which comfortably houses everything.\n\n6×4 works. You could also go 5×4 if grid real estate is tight, but controls would be more compact.\n\n**10. ResizeObserver:** Confirmed, will spec it that way.\n\n**11. Tap-to-center coordinate mapping:**\n\nBoth protocols support this well:\n\n- **VISCA:** Supports absolute position (`AbsolutePosition` command with pan/tilt coordinates). Combined with `CAM_PanTiltPosInq` to know current position, you can calculate the target. VISCA gives 16-bit signed pan/tilt positions spanning the camera's full mechanical range.\n- **NDI:** Supports `NDIlib_recv_ptz_pan_tilt(pan, tilt)` with absolute values in [-1.0, 1.0] range.\n\nThe math:\n1. Know current pan/tilt position (from last poll or last command)\n2. Know the camera's field of view at current zoom level (this is camera-specific — we'd need a FOV table or estimate, which could be a device configuration value)\n3. User taps at (x%, y%) from center of the video\n4. Calculate: `new_pan = current_pan + (x_offset% × horizontal_fov)`, same for tilt\n\n**Practical simplification:** Without exact FOV data, we can use a proportional approach — treat the visible frame as spanning some fraction of the total pan/tilt range at the current zoom level, and scale the offset accordingly. This won't be pixel-perfect but will be \"close enough\" — the volunteer can tap again or use the D-pad to fine-tune. This is how PTZOptics Hive does it (\"click-to-center\").\n\nIf the camera doesn't report position (NDI-only without VISCA), tap-to-center can still work using the last-known commanded position as the reference.\n\n**12. Multiple cameras and bandwidth:**\n\n**Bandwidth math:**\n- A 1080p30 stream encoded at quality suitable for preview = ~3-5 Mbps per stream\n- Two streams = ~6-10 Mbps\n- WiFi 6 practical per-client throughput on 5GHz = 200-600 Mbps depending on distance/interference\n\n**Verdict:** Two simultaneous preview streams are well within WiFi 6 capability. Three or four would also work. The bottleneck is more likely to be the server's CPU for multiple FFmpeg transcodes than WiFi bandwidth.\n\n**Recommendation:** \n- Allow the widget to show **one camera at a time** via a dropdown selector (if multiple cameras are configured)\n- Combined with the OBS preview widget, that's 2 concurrent video streams to a single tablet — completely fine on WiFi 6\n- Don't limit it architecturally though — if someone wants two camera widgets on a large display, let them. The fan-out architecture handles it (same FFmpeg process, just another WebSocket subscriber)\n\nThe dropdown makes sense from a UX perspective too — on a tablet-sized viewport, two full camera control widgets would be too cramped.\n\n---\n\n## Feature Set Additions\n\nGiven the protocol capabilities, I'd suggest adding one more feature to your list for the spec:\n\n- **home** — Both VISCA (`81 01 06 04 FF`) and NDI support a \"home\" position reset. Useful as a panic button for volunteers.\n\nI would **not** add white balance/exposure/gain to the initial spec. Those are important but are set-and-forget during installation, not adjusted by volunteers during service. They can be a future admin-only addition.\n\n---\n\n## Summary of Decisions for the Spec\n\n| Question | Decision |\n|---|---|\n| Video delivery | fMP4 over dedicated WebSocket, MSE in browser |\n| Latency target | Sub-500ms for both OBS and camera |\n| Multiple clients | Single FFmpeg per source, server fans out to subscribers |\n| OBS no-feed state | \"No Active Stream or Recording\" when neither active |\n| Protocol | Interface abstracts NDI + VISCA; admin chooses per camera |\n| Continuous movement | Press-and-hold with 200ms keepalive, 500ms dead-man timeout |\n| Zoom poll interval | 2s via VISCA inquiry (NDI-only tracks last-commanded) |\n| Preset storage | Our database (with absolute position recall — smooth motion guaranteed) |\n| Camera widget size | 6×4 in seed-dashboard |\n| OBS preview widget size | 2×2 in seed-dashboard |\n| Controls visibility | ResizeObserver per established pattern |\n| Tap-to-center | Proportional offset from center using known position + estimated FOV |\n| Multiple cameras | Dropdown selector in widget; 1 camera feed per widget instance; architecturally supports N subscribers |\n| Additional feature | Add `home` to feature set |\n\nAny other questions or adjustments before I write the spec?"

                    "kind": "text",
                    "data": "**6. Pan/tilt speed:**\n\nTwo options:\n\n- **Fixed speed:** Pick a sensible default (e.g., 50% of max) that works for most framing adjustments. Simple, predictable for volunteers.\n- **Adaptive speed based on zoom level:** Move slower when zoomed in (fine adjustments), faster when zoomed out (coarse re-framing). This is how most professional PTZ controllers work and dramatically reduces overshoot at high zoom.\n\nI'd recommend **adaptive speed tied to current zoom level** as the default behavior. The formula is straightforward: `speed = MAX_SPEED * (1 - zoomLevel * DAMPING_FACTOR)`. At wide angle you get fast movement; at telephoto you get precise control. The volunteer doesn't have to think about it — it just feels right.\n\nWe wouldn't expose a speed slider to the user. The system handles it automatically. Admins could configure min/max speed bounds per camera if needed, but that's a future refinement.\n\n**8. Commands + onboard preset — conflicts and undefined content:**\n\n**Conflicts:** No issues. If we send an absolute position command AND also recall an onboard preset, whichever arrives last wins. Since we're using our own database presets (recalling via absolute position commands), we'd never accidentally trigger an onboard preset recall. The two systems are independent.\n\nIf we *did* want to mirror to onboard storage as a backup: we'd store (write to camera) at preset-creation time, and only recall from our DB via absolute commands at runtime. No conflict.\n\n**What's stored in camera onboard presets:** This is **not** well-defined across cameras. The VISCA spec only guarantees pan/tilt/zoom position. Focus is camera-dependent — some store it, some don't. AI tracking state, white balance, exposure settings — all vendor-specific. PTZOptics cameras store pan/tilt/zoom/focus. Cheaper cameras may only store pan/tilt/zoom.\n\nThis is exactly why storing in our database is the right call:\n- We define exactly what a preset contains (the list you specified: pan, tilt, zoom, focus, auto-focus, AI tracking, disable-tilt, disable-zoom)\n- If a camera can't report a value (e.g., focus position inquiry fails), we gracefully omit it from the snapshot — the preset just won't restore that axis\n- Every preset has consistent, predictable content regardless of camera vendor\n- The system explicitly knows what it stored vs. what it couldn't capture\n\n**12. CPU overload escape hatches (for your awareness, not spec):**\n\nSeveral tricks before needing more hardware:\n\n1. **Reduce preview resolution/framerate:** Instead of passing through 1080p30, tell FFmpeg to scale to 720p or even 540p and drop to 15fps for previews. `-vf scale=960:540 -r 15` cuts CPU by ~60%. The preview is small on the dashboard anyway — the volunteer won't notice.\n\n2. **Hardware-accelerated encoding:** If the server has an Intel CPU with Quick Sync (most modern Intel chips), use `-c:v h264_qsv` or `-c:v h264_vaapi` instead of software encoding. Near-zero CPU cost. NVIDIA has NVENC. This is the single biggest win.\n\n3. **Copy mode when possible:** For OBS preview specifically, the RTMP relay already has H.264 — if the browser can handle the codec/container, we can remux without re-encoding (`-c:v copy`). MSE with fMP4 supports this for H.264 sources. Zero transcoding CPU.\n\n4. **Lazy startup:** Only spawn FFmpeg when a client subscribes. No clients = no CPU spent on preview streams.\n\n5. **Quality presets:** FFmpeg's `-preset ultrafast` trades file size for speed. For a LAN preview that's immediately discarded, we don't care about compression efficiency.\n\n6. **Offload to a second machine:** If the server is truly maxed, you could run the preview transcoding on a separate Raspberry Pi 5 or mini PC that receives NDI/RTMP and serves WebSocket previews. The main server just proxies the WebSocket connection. No architectural rework needed — just a config change pointing to a different preview endpoint.\n\nIn practice, for 2-3 preview streams on a modern i5/i7, options 3+4 alone (copy mode for OBS + lazy startup) should keep CPU negligible.                     "data": "**8.** Makes sense. Each preset in our DB will have a `storedOnCamera: boolean` flag (and optionally the camera's onboard preset slot number). When recalling:\n- If `storedOnCamera: true` → issue the camera's native preset recall command (smooth MotionSync on cameras that support it)\n- If `storedOnCamera: false` → issue absolute position commands from our DB values\n\nWhen creating a preset with `storedOnCamera: true`, we write to both our DB and the camera's onboard slot. This gives you the option to leverage the camera's native smooth recall when available, while still having our DB as the source of truth for what the preset *should* contain.\n\n**12.** Yes — 720p as the default preview resolution makes sense. The widget is at most ~540px wide on the dashboard; sending 1080p would be downscaled by the browser anyway, wasting bandwidth and CPU for no visual benefit. We'll define a code constant like `PREVIEW_RESOLUTION = { width: 1280, height: 720 }` that can be changed without code restructuring.\n\nFor hardware acceleration: yes, we can detect at startup whether VA-API (Linux/Intel), QSV, or NVENC is available by probing FFmpeg's encoder list (`ffmpeg -encoders`). If a hardware encoder is present, use it; otherwise fall back to `libx264 -preset ultrafast`. This is a one-time startup probe — the result is cached for the lifetime of the process.\n\nBoth of these (720p default, hardware detection, no-subscriber = no FFmpeg) will be in the spec.\n\n---\n\nNo further questions. I have a clear picture of both features. I'll write the requirements spec now."

The proportional speed from distance-from-center is much more natural on a touch device, and diagonal movement is inherent rather than requiring simultaneous button presses.\n\n10. **Req 5.3 — Dead-zone (15%), speed quantization (0.05), and stale-session handling** — These prevent real problems: finger tremor jitter, servo hunting, and ghost movements after reconnect.\n\n11. **Req 6.8 — Preset timeout 10s** — Changed from 5s with rationale about mechanical PTZ traverse time.                 "content": [
                  {
                    "kind": "text",
                    "data": "Good, I've re-read the full spec. Now let me address your questions:\n\n---\n\n**1. Reconnect tap behavior for preview:**\n\nNo, I don't think we need a separate \"tap to reconnect\" requirement. The existing spec (Req 2.11) already has automatic reconnection with exponential backoff. Unlike the OBS WebSocket disconnect (where the *backend* needs user intervention to re-enter a password or re-configure), the preview WebSocket failures are purely transport-level — the server is still running, it's just a dropped connection. The automatic reconnect handles it without user action.\n\nHowever, if the reconnection reaches max backoff (10s intervals) and keeps failing, the widget will show the \"unhealthy\" indicator. At that point, a page refresh resets everything. If you want, we *could* add: \"After 3 consecutive failed reconnection attempts, show a 'Tap to Retry' button that resets the backoff and immediately attempts reconnection.\" But I think that's polish, not a core requirement. Your call.\n\n**2. Dead-man's switch triggers, but keepalives resume:**\n\nThe current spec says after the dead-man timeout, the backend stops the camera and deletes the session. Then keepalives arrive for a session that no longer exists. Per Req 5.3: \"stale keepalives from a previous session are ignored.\"\n\nBut the *real* question is: should the backend auto-resume movement when keepalives start arriving again after a dropout? Options:\n\n- **A. Current spec (ignore stale keepalives):** After timeout, movement is dead. The volunteer must lift their finger and re-touch to initiate a new `move:start`. This is safest — the volunteer is forced to confirm intent.\n- **B. Auto-resume on keepalive after timeout:** Backend treats a keepalive after a timed-out session as an implicit new `move:start`. Smoother UX during brief dropouts, but riskier — the volunteer may not realize their finger is still on the joystick after a network blip.\n- **C. Auto-resume with a grace window:** If keepalives resume within 2 seconds of the dead-man stop, auto-resume. After 2 seconds, require a fresh `move:start`.\n\nI'd recommend **A (current spec)**. The volunteer sees the camera stop and the preview stalls briefly during the dropout. When the connection restores, the joystick indicator is still showing their finger position — they just lift and re-press to resume. This is the least surprising behavior and the safest.\n\n**3. Tap-to-center without VISCA:**\n\nYou're right to question this. Without VISCA inquiry, the backend tracks \"last-commanded\" position — and with the joystick, those last-commanded values are *speeds*, not positions. The backend issues `panTiltSpeed(0.3, -0.2)` — it knows the camera was moving, but not where it ended up.\n\nThere are two sub-cases:\n\n- **After absolute commands (preset activate, previous tap-to-center):** The last-commanded absolute position is accurate. Tap-to-center works fine.\n- **After joystick movement:** The position is unknown. We'd have to integrate speed × time, which is wildly inaccurate due to variable camera response time and acceleration curves.\n\n**Recommendation:** Tap-to-center should be **disabled when the last position source was joystick movement (relative) and no VISCA is configured.** Specifically: the backend tracks a `positionConfidence: \"absolute\" | \"estimated\"` flag. After an absolute command (preset, tap-to-center) it's `absolute`. After any relative speed command it's `estimated`. When `estimated` and no VISCA: tap-to-center shows a Toast: \"Tap-to-center unavailable — use a preset to re-calibrate position, or add VISCA for accurate tracking.\" This avoids wild camera jumps.\n\nShould I encode this into the spec?\n\n**4. Video size in expanded mode:**\n\nYou're right — Req 4.4 is ambiguous. The \"2×2-cell-equivalent\" in Req 4.4b was meant as the *minimum* space the video needs (for threshold calculation), not a cap on its actual rendered size. Req 4.7 correctly says \"occupy a fixed portion of the widget (left side)\" which fills available height. I'll fix Req 4.4b to clarify the threshold logic vs. actual rendering.\n\n**5. Dead-zone indicator:**\n\nYes, a subtle visual indicator would help. I'd suggest a small circle or ring at 15% radius rendered with `color-border` (very subtle, semi-transparent) — enough that the volunteer can see \"if I'm inside this ring, nothing happens\" without it being distracting. The indicator dot would snap into the dead-zone visually when released. Should I add this?\n\n**6. Req 6.2 — visual indicator on last preset:**\n\nRe-reading the current Req 6.2: \"The button for the activated preset SHALL highlight using `color-primary` to indicate it is the active preset.\"\n\nThat IS a visual indicator on the last-tapped preset. Are you saying we should NOT highlight the active preset at all? Or is the concern something else? The intent was: if the volunteer taps \"Pulpit\" and then 5 minutes later glances at the controls, the highlight tells them which preset they last activated (assuming they haven't manually moved since). It clears on any manual movement (Req 6.6).\n\nIf you don't want this — we can remove the highlight entirely and just rely on the Toast for feedback.\n\n**7. Sort order — drag to reorder:**\n\nMakes sense. The admin drags presets into order in the preset list, and the backend assigns `sortOrder` values (e.g., 0, 1, 2...) based on the resulting order. I'll update Req 7.5/7.6 to use drag-to-reorder and remove the \"Sort Order number input\" from the preset modal.\n\n**8. How to tell the camera to disable tilt/zoom in AI tracking:**\n\nThis is camera-firmware-specific. Looking at the Tongveo TV-NVS20A-4KN and similar AI-tracking PTZ cameras:\n\n- Most AI-tracking cameras expose these as **configuration parameters accessible via their web UI or proprietary API** (HTTP CGI commands), not standard VISCA/NDI commands.\n- The NDI SDK doesn't have standard commands for \"disable tilt tracking\" or \"disable zoom tracking\" — those aren't in the PTZ command set.\n- Some cameras expose this via vendor-specific VISCA extensions or HTTP endpoints (e.g., `http://{ip}/cgi-bin/param.cgi?action=set&group=tracking&tilt_enable=0`).\n\n**Options:**\n- **A. HTTP CGI commands:** Most PTZ cameras with AI tracking expose a REST-like API for tracking configuration. The backend could send HTTP requests to the camera's web interface.\n- **B. Vendor-specific VISCA commands:** Some cameras extend VISCA with proprietary bytes for tracking control.\n- **C. NDI metadata messages:** Some cameras accept XML metadata for configuration.\n\n**Recommendation:** The `CameraControlInterface` should add `setAiTracking(enabled)`, `setAiTrackingTiltDisable(enabled)`, `setAiTrackingZoomDisable(enabled)` as abstract methods. The implementation is camera-specific — for the initial Tongveo camera, we'd implement these via HTTP CGI calls to the camera's web API. The interface remains protocol-agnostic; individual driver implementations know how to talk to their specific camera's tracking system.\n\nThis means the driver isn't purely NDI or VISCA — it's an `NdiCameraDriver` that *also* knows the camera's HTTP API endpoint for AI tracking control. The admin would provide the camera's web interface IP (which is likely the same as the VISCA IP) during setup. Should I add this to the spec, or keep it as an implementation detail deferred to the design doc?\n\n---\n\n**Summary of proposed changes:**\n1. No change (auto-reconnect is sufficient), unless you want \"tap to retry\" after repeated failures\n2. No change needed — current spec (Option A) is correct\n3. Add position-confidence tracking and disable tap-to-center when position is estimated (NDI-only after joystick use)\n4. Fix Req 4.4b wording to clarify threshold vs. rendering\n5. Add subtle dead-zone ring indicator\n6. Awaiting your answer — keep highlight or remove it?\n7. Change sort order to drag-to-reorder in admin\n8. Add HTTP CGI/vendor API as the mechanism, exposed via abstract interface methods"
                  }

                    "data": "All changes applied.                 "role": "assistant",
                "content": [
                  {
                    "kind": "text",
                    "data": "Based on the Tongveo/Tenveo product listings and similar cameras:\n\n**Presenter Tracking** — The camera uses AI (face + body recognition) to follow a single person as they move around the stage. The camera pans, tilts, and zooms to keep that person centered in frame. If the person leaves the field of view entirely, the camera returns to a \"home\" position and waits for them to reappear.\n\n**Auto-Framing** — Instead of physically panning/tilting the camera, it uses the full sensor (often at a wider angle) and digitally crops/zooms to frame the subject. The camera body stays still — only the digital crop window moves. This is smoother but you lose optical resolution since you're cropping a portion of the sensor.\n\nSome cameras in this tier (like the Newegg listing for the Tongveo NDI) also mention a third mode:\n\n**Zone Tracking** — You define preset zones (areas of the stage). When the subject moves from one zone to another, the camera transitions to the corresponding preset position. This is less \"following\" and more \"switching between predetermined shots based on where the person is.\"\n\nFor our spec purposes: the Tongveo appears to expose **Presenter Tracking on/off** and **Auto-Framing on/off** as the two modes — selectable via the camera's web interface. What we're calling \"AI Tracking\" in our spec would map to enabling Presenter Tracking. The \"Disable Zoom\" concept would mean switching from Presenter Tracking (which zooms to follow) to something more constrained — but the camera doesn't expose that as a separate toggle; it's baked into the mode selection.\n\nDoes this change how you want to model the AI tracking toggles, or are you comfortable with the current approach (keep them in the feature set, disable the ones this camera can't do)?"
                  }

                    "kind": "text",
                    "data": "\nGood questions. Let me address each:\n\n**1. Metadata JSON blob instead of new columns:**\n\nYou're right. Looking at the existing schema, `device_connections` already has a `metadata` JSON column designed for device-type-specific fields. Camera config (ndiSourceName, fovWideAngle, cameraModel, cameraFeatures, aiHttpCookie, aiCredentialId) should go there rather than adding 7+ nullable columns that only cameras use. I'll fix this.\n\n**2. Presets in metadata vs. separate table:**\n\nI'd recommend keeping presets in a separate table for these reasons:\n- Presets have their own CRUD lifecycle (create/edit/delete/reorder independently of the device config)\n- A separate table gives us indexing, cascade delete, and cleaner queries\n- The metadata blob would become very large with multiple presets each containing 12+ fields\n- Preset reorder is a `PUT /presets/order` — surgically updating a nested array in a JSON blob requires read-modify-write (race condition prone in SQLite without row locks)\n\nThe metadata JSON blob works well for config that changes rarely and is always read/written as a unit. Presets are more like child entities with their own lifecycles.\n\n**3. Reuse host/port for VISCA:**\n\nGood catch. Since cameras use NDI as the primary protocol and VISCA is just for position polling (same IP, different port), we can store the camera's IP in `host` and the VISCA port in `port`. The `ndiSourceName` goes in metadata. This eliminates the \"store 127.0.0.1/0\" hack entirely. When VISCA is not configured, `host` and `port` would be... hmm, but those columns are NOT NULL. We'd need a sentinel value still for cameras without VISCA. OR we make VISCA optional by checking if `host` is empty string vs. an actual IP. What's cleaner: empty string sentinel, or just always requiring a host (even if VISCA isn't used, the camera has an IP)?\n\nActually — the camera always has an IP (it's on the network for NDI), and the AI HTTP API also uses that same IP. So `host` = camera's IP (always populated), `port` = VISCA port (5500 default, used if VISCA is enabled). Whether VISCA polling is enabled can be a boolean in metadata (`viscaEnabled: true/false`). This is clean.\n\n**4. ndiAvailable in Zustand:**\n\nYou're right — since NDI is now required for all cameras (Req 3.4 says cameras without NDI are not supported), and if NDI isn't available no cameras will even appear, this flag is redundant for the camera widget. It was there from the earlier design where NDI was optional. It should be removed from the camera slice. The only place `ndiAvailable` matters is the admin page (to show \"NDI SDK not installed\" warning) — and that can come from the initial state payload without being in the camera zustand slice.\n\n**5. Disabled dropdown vs hidden:**\n\nMakes sense — disabled with one value is more consistent and tells the volunteer \"this is a camera selector, there's just one.\" I'll update.\n\n**6. ConnectingOverlay across controls in expanded mode:**\n\nGood point. If the camera is offline/connecting, the controls are non-functional anyway. Showing the overlay across the entire widget (video + controls) rather than just the video section makes it clear that nothing works until the connection is established. I'll update.\n\n**7. ion-range instead of input type=\"range\":**\n\nYou're right. For consistency with the Ionic component library used throughout. Let me check for other base elements that should be Ionic:\n- Zoom slider: `<input type=\"range\">` → `<ion-range>`\n- Focus slider: same fix\n- Camera model dropdown in admin: should be `<IonSelect>` (already described as IonSelect for the camera switcher)\n- Preset name input: should be `<IonInput>`\n- FOV input: `<IonInput type=\"number\">`\n- Toggle buttons are already specified as Ionic toggles ✓\n- Joystick: custom component (no Ionic equivalent) ✓\n\n**8. Remove caution note from admin UI:**\n\nWill do — keep it in setup docs only.\n\n**9. Many CTS commands vs. single state-update command:**\n\nCurrent approach: `cts:camera:zoom:set`, `cts:camera:focus:auto`, `cts:camera:focus:set`, `cts:camera:ai-tracking:set`, `cts:camera:ai-tilt:set`, `cts:camera:ai-zoom:set` — 6 separate events for what are all \"set a value on the camera.\"\n\n**Alternative: Single `cts:camera:set` with partial state:**\n```typescript\nsocket.emit(\"cts:camera:set\", { cameraId, zoom: 0.5 });\nsocket.emit(\"cts:camera:set\", { cameraId, aiTracking: true });\nsocket.emit(\"cts:camera:set\", { cameraId, focus: 0.3 });\n```\n\nAnything undefined = not changed. This is the pattern used by React's `setState` and most REST PATCH endpoints.\n\n**My recommendation: Consolidate.** Reasons:\n- Fewer event constants to maintain\n- The handler logic is the same either way (switch on which fields are present)\n- Presets already set multiple values atomically — the single-event pattern is more natural for that\n- Less surface area for typos in event names\n- The PTZ move events (`start`/`keepalive`/`stop`) should stay separate because they have fundamentally different semantics (continuous vs. fire-once)\n\nSo the final event set would be:\n- `cts:camera:ptz:move:start` / `keepalive` / `stop` — continuous movement (stays as-is)\n- `cts:camera:set` — fire-once state changes: `{ cameraId, zoom?, focus?, autoFocus?, aiTracking?, aiTilt?, aiZoom? }`\n- `cts:camera:preset:activate` — stays separate (has its own response flow with Toast)\n- `cts:camera:ptz:tap-to-center` — stays separate (takes offset coordinates, not a state value)\n\nThis reduces 6 events → 1 for the \"set a value\" category, while keeping the semantically distinct ones separate. Complexity-wise it's lower: one handler with a simple `if (payload.zoom !== undefined) setZoom(...)` pattern vs. 6 separate handler registrations.\n\n---\n\nWant me to apply all 9 changes to the design doc now?"

                  {
                    "kind": "text",
                    "data": "You're understanding it correctly — `fovWideAngle` is the horizontal field of view at full wide (zoom = 0.0).\n\nThe spec currently uses a linear approximation for the effective FOV at any zoom level:\n\n```\neffectiveFov = fovWideAngle * (1.0 - zoomLevel)\n```\n\nThis means at full telephoto (zoom = 1.0), the effective FOV = 0°, which is obviously wrong — the camera still sees *something* at full zoom. A real camera's FOV at full telephoto is determined by its optical zoom ratio. For the Tongveo NVS20A-4KN with 20x optical zoom:\n\n- Wide: ~60° horizontal FOV\n- Telephoto: ~60° / 20 = ~3° horizontal FOV\n\nSo yes, there **is** a mathematical relationship. If we know the zoom ratio (20x for this camera), we can derive the telephoto FOV:\n\n```\nfovAtZoom = fovWideAngle / (1 + zoomLevel * (opticalZoomRatio - 1))\n```\n\nAt zoom = 0: `60 / 1 = 60°`\nAt zoom = 1: `60 / 20 = 3°`\n\nThis is more accurate than the linear formula. The only extra field needed is `opticalZoomRatio` (e.g., 20 for 20x zoom) — which is a fixed property of the camera model, not something that changes. We could either:\n\n1. **Store it in metadata** alongside `fovWideAngle` — admin enters both (or just the zoom ratio, since FOV wide can be looked up per model)\n2. **Derive it from the camera model** — if it's \"Tongveo NVS20A-4KN\", we know it's 20x. Generic cameras would need it specified.\n\nEither way, the admin doesn't need to specify `fovTelephoto` separately — it's `fovWide / zoomRatio`.\n\n**My recommendation:** Replace `fovWideAngle` with two fields in metadata: `fovWideAngle` (default 60) and `opticalZoomRatio` (default 20). Update the tap-to-center formula to the correct one above. Both are easily found on the camera's spec sheet. Want me to make this change?"
                  }

      "version": "v1",
      "kind": "Prompt",
      "data": {
        "message_id": "6dc312a9-ac2a-4000-a75e-4d1e008bef3b",
        "content": [
          {
            "kind": "text",
            "data": "Within your working directory you'll find our core project (livestream-control-system) and two extensions (multi-platform-streaming and lower-thirds). We need to write a spec that adds two more features to the overall system. We'll call this spec video-control-and-preview. Our features are\n1. Show and hear what OBS is streaming on the dashboard\n2. Show and control and NDI camera that's on the network\n\n#1 should be fairly straight forward. We'll need the backend to send the stream of video and audio, and we'll need a widget (setup the seed-dashboard.ts script with it being 2x2) to show it. The widget's status will be that we're receiving OBS' feed, and we'll name the status \"Feed\". The widget should overlay the bottom right of the video with a WCAG 48x48px sound icon that's semi-transparent that allows the user to control if the dashboard will actually play the audio. Audio should be muted by default, and re-mute if the dashboard is refreshed. The video should auto-fit to the widget's size, without stretching the video, and center horiontally or vertically depending on the size of the video. E.g. if it's a portrait video, then the height should be the height of the widget, and the width should match the stream, and then be centered in the widget from there. Same idea if the video is in landscape, it should be centered vertically. If the user taps the video outside of the mute button, the the video preview should open up in a large modal, that just has a dismiss button, and a title of Stream Preview. Open question: should we, based on the viewport, downscale the video before sending it to the dashboard to save on wifi bandwidth, or is it not worth the CPU compute power given all the things the server is already doing, including multiple streams.\n\n#2 is a lot more involved. We're going to need a new type of service that can talk with an NDI camera. We'll need an interface for talking to cameras in general, and we'll need a feature set. The available features are [pan, tilt, zoom, focus, ai-tracking, ai-tracking-zoom-disable, ai-tracking-tilt-disable] (Open question: are there any other feature sets we should consider at this time?). From the user's perspective for the dashboard, we'll need a video preview (this is different from #1 because it's JUST the video, without anything else in the way that we might have setup in OBS). When the widget is small, it will just be the video preview, and when tapped, it will open into a modal with the controls described. But when it's big enough then the controls should be visible in the widget. For the controls, we're going to need the ability to toggle auto-focus, and if auto-focus is disabled, then the ability to manually focus (admin/power-users only) and the ability to choose (from a dropdown) a specific focus point, if any are avaiable (disabled dropdown otherwise). A Pan/Tilt controls, setup like a remote with a gap in the middle. And an absolute position zoom slider (this should be longer to give more control). We'll also want the abilit to see a list of presets (3 tall, but scrolls if there are more) with single tap \"Activate\" buttons. Here is a loose diagram of the widget / modal.\n\nXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX ^ /\\ +------------+ \nX X | /__\\ | Auto Focus | \nX X | /| |\\ +------------+ \nX X | \\| __ |/ \nX Video Preview X \\ / <-- Focus ---> \nX X Z \\/ \nX X O +------------------------+\nX X O |Preset 1 Activate |\nXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX M +------------------------+\n+------------+ +------------+ |Preset 2 Activate |\n|Disable Tilt| |Disable Zoom| | +------------------------+\n+------------+ +------------+ | |Preset 3 Activate |\n+-----------+ v +------------------------+\n|AI Tracking| \n+-----------+ \n\nWhen we say that the modal is \"big enough\" we mean that the video can fit into a 2x2 slot (centered like the OBS preview) AND has room for all the buttons around it. All buttons and sliders will have a 36px tall footprint (or wide for the zoom slider) The focus driver will be greyed out if auto focus is on. Both the auto-focus button and driver will be hidden when the user is just a volunteer. The pan/tilt buttons should be styled, but have a reasonable 48x48 size footprint (this can be not exact if we have more of a trapezoid/triangual touch point), and the preset Activate buttons should be 36px tall. With appropriate paddings. \n\nWhen the controls are visible, I'd really like the ability for the volunteer to tap on the video, and for us to extrapolate the coordinates, and then auto move the camera to be centered on that point. If Disable Tilt is enabled (Note: Disable Title, AI Tracking, Disable Zoom, and Auto Focus should have the 36px tall footprint, but also be toggles not buttons), then we should only pan based on where they touched. If AI tracking is enabled, the touch should do nothing, but there should be a toast message to tell the user that tapping to shift the angle is disable when AI tracking is on. Presets shift all controls based on what the admin configured for the preset. If a preset has been activated AND no changes have been made, then the button should be disabled and show \"Activated\". We will not worry about figuring out if the camera settings match a preset if the server has been restarted. The button should show Activating and be disabled while we're waiting for the camrea settings to take effect. We should communicate failures via a toast message if we fail to set the settings, and re-allow the user to activate again.\n\nIf the controls are not visible, the video should expand to fit the size of the widget, and center like the OBS video preview. Tapping on the video should open a large modal that has all the controls available. The widget's status should be based on having a connection with the camera.\n\nFor the admin devices page, the admin will need the ability to add the camera from the network. The admin will also need the ability to set what features are avaiable for the camera, by using toggles by each item. When the admin adds a preset, a modal should open that shows the same controls (except the presets) as the widget. The modal should have a \"snapshot\" button that captures the cameras settings. For each setting, here's how we know what to store\n- Auto-Focus: Based on the toggle in the modal\n- Focus Position: Polled from the camera, only polled and stored if auto-focus is off. Gracefully fails if the VISCA or NDI protocols can't provide the data\n- Disable Tilt: Based on the toggle in the modal\n- Disable Zoom: Based on the toggle in the modal\n- AI Tracking: Based on the toggle in the modal\n- Zoom: Polled from the camera. Gracefully fails if the VISCA or NDI protocols can't provide the data\n- Pan: Polled from the camera. Gracefully fails if the VISCA or NDI protocols can't provide the data\n- Tilt: Polled from the camera. Gracefully fails if the VISCA or NDI protocols can't provide the data\n\nFor the widget, we should update the seed-dashboard.ts file to have a widget that should be large enough (Will 6x4 work?)\n\nAny questions or clarifications before you start writing the requirements?"
          }
        ],
        "meta": {
          "timestamp": 1780462030
        }
      }

      "version": "v1",
      "kind": "AssistantMessage",
      "data": {
        "message_id": "0c48639e-bf8c-42b4-a870-749f51b731c1",
        "content": [
          {
            "kind": "text",
            "data": "This is a great feature breakdown. Before I start writing the spec, I have several questions and observations:\n\n## OBS Stream Preview (#1)\n\n**On the open question (downscaling):**\n\nI'd recommend **not** re-encoding on the server. You're already running FFmpeg forwarders for multi-platform streaming. Adding another transcode pipeline for preview would compete for CPU with the actual stream forwarding. Instead, I'd suggest:\n\n- Sending the RTMP stream from the relay as-is via WebSocket (using something like `fluent-ffmpeg` to remux to fragmented MP4/WebM for browser playback)\n- Or using HLS with a short segment duration (~1-2s) for slightly delayed but bandwidth-friendly preview\n\n**Questions:**\n\n1. **Latency tolerance** — Is near-real-time important (sub-2s), or is a 3-5s delay acceptable for the preview? This determines whether we go WebSocket-based (lower latency, more bandwidth) or HLS (more efficient, higher latency).\n\n2. **Multiple clients** — If multiple tablets have the dashboard open, should they all get the preview stream? This affects whether we remux once and fan out, or remux per-client.\n\n3. **Stream absence** — When OBS isn't streaming (or the relay has no input), should the widget show a static \"No Feed\" state, or should the widget container's status indicator handle that (showing \"Feed: Disconnected\")?\n\n## NDI Camera Control (#2)\n\n**On the open question (additional features):**\n\nConsider these additions:\n- **White balance** (auto/manual/presets like 3200K/5600K) — common in church environments with mixed lighting\n- **Exposure/gain** — important when stage lighting changes between worship and sermon\n- **Iris/aperture** — related to exposure, often toggled auto/manual like focus\n\nHowever, these might be better deferred to a later iteration since they're less critical for basic camera operation. Your call.\n\n**Clarifying questions:**\n\n4. **NDI protocol vs VISCA-over-NDI** — Are we targeting cameras that expose PTZ control via NDI's built-in PTZ protocol, VISCA-over-IP, or both? The spec mentions both VISCA and NDI — should the interface abstract over both, with the admin selecting the control protocol during device setup?\n\n5. **NDI video feed delivery** — NDI is a LAN protocol. For the camera preview, are we expecting the backend to receive the NDI feed and transcode/relay it to the browser (similar to OBS preview), or is there another path? NDI isn't browser-native, so we'd need server-side conversion.\n\n6. **Pan/tilt speed** — For the directional pad, should holding the button continuously move (press-and-hold for velocity), or is each tap a discrete step? Same question for the tap-to-center: does it issue an absolute position command, or a relative move?\n\n7. **Zoom slider \"absolute position\"** — Does this mean we need to poll the camera's current zoom level on connect and keep the slider in sync? What happens if the zoom is changed externally (e.g., via a hardware controller)?\n\n8. **Preset storage** — You mention \"snapshot captures the camera's settings.\" Are presets stored in our database only, or also written to the camera's internal preset memory? Some NDI/VISCA cameras have onboard preset slots.\n\n9. **6×4 widget size** — In the 10×6 grid, 6×4 leaves 4 columns and 2 rows for other widgets. That gives room for the OBS preview (2×2) and the OBS controls widget (currently 4×3 per the existing spec). Want me to validate whether that all fits, or are you planning to adjust the OBS controls widget size?\n\n10. **\"Big enough\" threshold** — You said controls show when the widget can fit video in a 2×2 slot plus room for controls. Should I calculate the exact column/row threshold where this kicks in, or should the spec just define a pixel/rem breakpoint and let the component use `ResizeObserver` (per the established pattern)?\n\n11. **Tap-to-center coordinate mapping** — This requires knowing the camera's field of view and current position to translate a pixel tap into a pan/tilt absolute position. Should we assume the camera reports its current absolute pan/tilt values, and that we can calculate the target based on the tap offset from center? Or is there a simpler \"relative move toward tap\" approach you'd prefer?\n\n12. **Multi-camera future** — Should the spec account for multiple NDI cameras on the network (each getting its own widget instance), or is this single-camera for now?\n\n---\n\nOnce you answer these, I'll have everything I need to write a comprehensive spec covering the backend services, frontend widgets, admin UI, database schema, socket events, and test strategy."
          }
        ]
      }
    },
    {
      "version": "v1",
      "kind": "Prompt",
      "data": {
        "message_id": "4d5aeab0-ed18-4868-bb74-55167ec724e1",
        "content": [
          {
            "kind": "text",
            "data": "Got it on downscaling, but we REALLY want the previews to be live so that there's no noticable delay between the volunteering making a change (e.g. activating a lower third) and them seeing that on their preview. If we're going to stream over a websocket, it should be a different socket than our command socket, so we can debug more easily.\n\n1. We want things to be as closer to realtime as possible for OBS. For the camera, realtime is imperative. Otherwise the volunteer will overshoot on some of their controls (e.g. pan too far)\n2. All clients that are requesting the stream should get he same stream (so if a dashbaord doesn't have the widget, we shouldn't send it, but two people on the same dashboard with both widgets would both get the same stream)\n3. Let's go with \"No Active Stream or Recording\", and if either are active, we want the preview.\n\nFor the controls, I think that depends on the camera we're starting with. Do not over index or focus too much in on the camera we're starting with. Do not make architectural decisions based on the starting camera. Assume that NDI and VISCA protocols, but it should be able to work with a camera that just has one. Are starting target camera is the Tongveo TV-NVS20A-4KN. All planning and architectural decisions should be based on protocols, not a specific camera. Do not over index on that camera model.\n\n4. I like supporting both, but letting the admin choosing which one. The system should be smart enough to detect and let the admin know if their protocol of choice isn't supported by the camera\n5. Yes, the server will have direct LAN access to the camera, but then the server will need to turn that into something it can send to the dashboard\n6. Holding the button should result in continuous movement. To ensure a network drop doesnt just spin the camera, we should model the communication with a \"still alive\" mechanism so that the backend stops if it fails to see the end message. We want the motion to be smooth. Panning and tilting with the buttons is relative.\n7. Zoom is absolute. We will need to do a reasonable poll (every 2s? Slower? Faster? We don't want to overwhelm the network) to ensure the zoom slider stays in sync, even if it's changed through another system, or another user connected to the camera\n8. Can we tell if the camera will support the onboard storage? Can we tell how much of the data the camera can store? Is there any any risk of non-smooth motion (e.g. pan, then tilt, instead of panning and tilting) if we only store it in our database?\n9. Based on our paddings and grid size, what is the smallest we can go? From there I'll make a decision on where we want to start.\n10. Use the ResizeObserver per the established pattern\n11. Do most cameras with NDI and/or VISCA support this? What are the options based on the protocol(s) and typical features avaiable over those protocols?\n12. The spec should allow for multiple cameras. What kind of bandwidth concerns do we have though? Should we add a dropdown to the widget so a dashboard is only pulling two streams max at a time? (If there are multiple cameras, we can switch, but we can't view both on the same tablet). Or will typical Wi-Fi 6+ allow for multiple streams to the same device, in near realtime just fine?"
          }
        ],
        "meta": {
          "timestamp": 1780464512

      "version": "v1",

        "message_id": "0781c906-fab8-4f4d-9c14-1ee673adcd11",

          {
            "kind": "toolResult",
            "data": {
              "toolUseId": "tooluse_uaCKZT7OMCyLFHbFWhXFY9",
              "content": [
                {
                  "kind": "text",
                  "data": "If the timeout is zero, it will return immediately with a frame if there is one. If the timeout is not zero, it will wait for a frame up to the timeout duration specified and return if it gets one (if there is already a frame waiting when the call is made it returns that frame immediately). If a frame of the type requested has been received before the timeout occurs, the function will return the data type received. Frames returned to you by this function must be freed. **The following code** illustrates how one might receive audio and/or video based on what is available; it will wait one second before returning if no data was received. You are able, if you wish, to take the received video, audio, or metadata frames and free them on another thread to ensure there is no chance of dropping frames while receiving them. A short queue is maintained on the receiver to allow you to process incoming data in the fashion most convenient for your application. If you always process buffers faster than in real-time, this queue will always be empty, and you will be running at the lowest possible latency. `NDIlib_recv_capture_v3` may return the value `NDIlib_frame_type_status_change`, to indicate that the device’s properties have changed. Because connecting to a video source might take a few seconds, some of the properties of that device are not known immediately and might even change on the fly. For instance, when connecting to a PTZ camera, it might not be known for a few seconds that it supports the PTZ command set. When this does become known, the value `NDIlib_frame_type_status_change` is returned to indicate that you should recheck device properties. This value is currently sent when a source changes PTZ type, recording capabilities, or web user interface control. If you wish to determine whether any audio, video, or metadata frames have been dropped, you can call `NDIlib_recv_get_performance`, which will supply the total frame count and the number of frames that have been dropped because they could not be de-queued fast enough. If you wish to determine the current queue depths on audio, video, or metadata (to poll whether receiving a frame would immediately give a result), you can call `NDIlib_recv_get_queue`. `NDIlib_recv_get_no_connections` will return the number of connections that are currently active and can also be used to detect whether the video source you are connected to is currently online or not. Additional functions provided by the receive SDK allow metadata to be passed upstream to connected sources via `NDIlib_recv_send_metadata`. Much like the sending of metadata frames in the NDI Send SDK, this is passed as a `NDIlib_metadata_frame_t` structure that is to be sent. Tally information is handled via `NDIlib_recv_set_tally`. This will take a `NDIlib_tally_t` structure that can be used to define the program and preview visibility status. The tally status is retained within the receiver so that, even if a connection is lost, the tally state is correctly set when it is subsequently restored. Connection metadata is an important concept that allows you to “register” certain metadata messages so that each time a new connection is established, the up-stream source (normally an **NDI-SEND** user) receives those strings. Note that there are many reasons that connections might be lost and established at run time. For instance, if an NDI Sender goes offline, the connection is lost; if it comes back online at a later time, the connection would be re-established, and the connection metadata would be resent. Some standard connection strings are specified for connection metadata, as outlined in the next section. Connection metadata strings are added with `NDIlib_recv_add_connection_metadata` that takes an `NDIlib_metadata_frame_t structure`. To clear all connection metadata strings, allowing them to be replaced, call `NDIlib_recv_clear_connection_metadata`. **An example that illustrates how you can provide your product name to anyone who ever connects to you is provided below**. When using the [**NDI Advanced SDK**][61], it is possible to assign custom memory allocators for receiving that will allow you to provide user-controlled buffers that are decompressed. This might sometimes improve performance or allow you to receive frames into GPU-accessible buffers. ### Receiver User Interfaces\n\nA sender might provide an interface that allows configuration. For instance, an NDI converter device might offer an interface that allows its settings to be changed; or a PTZ camera might provide an interface that provides access to specific settings and mode values. These interfaces are provided via a web URL that you can host. For example, a converter device might have an NDI Advanced SDK web page that is served at a URL such as `http://192. 168. 1. 156/control/index. html`. In order to get this address, you simply call the function:\n\n> `const char* NDIlib_recv_get_web_control(NDIlib_recv_instance_t p_instance);`\n\nThis will return a string representing the URL, or `NULL` if there is no current URL associated with the sender in question. Because connections might take a few seconds, this string might not be available immediately after having called connect. To avoid the need to poll this setting, note that `NDIlib_recv_capture_v3` returns a value of `NDIlib_frame_type_status_change` when this setting is known (or when it has changed). The string returned is owned by your application until you call `NDIlib_recv_free_string`. You can then store this URL and provide it to an end user as the options for that device. For instance, a PTZ camera or an NDI conversion box might allow its settings to be configured using a hosted web interface. For sources indicating they support the ability to be configured, the NDI Studio Monitor tool this capability, as shown in the bottom-right corner of the image below. When you click this gear gadget, the application opens the web page specified by the sender. ### Receiver PTZ Control\n\nNDI standardizes the control of PTZ cameras. An NDI receiver will automatically sense whether the device it is connected to is a PTZ camera and whether it may be controlled automatically. When controlling a camera via NDI, all configuration of the camera is completely transparent to the NDI client, which will respond to a uniform set of standard commands with well-defined parameter ranges. For instance, the NDI Studio Monitor tool uses these commands to display on-screen PTZ controls when the current source is reported to be a camera that supports control. To determine whether the connection that you are on would respond to PTZ messages, you may simply ask the receiver whether this property is supported using the following call:\n\n> `bool NDIlib_recv_ptz_is_supported(NDIlib_recv_instance_t p_instance)`;\n\nThis will return true when the video source is a PTZ system, and false otherwise. Note that connections are not instantaneous, so you might need to wait a few seconds after connection before the source indicates that it supports PTZ control. To avoid the need to poll this setting, note that `NDIlib_recv_capture_v3` returns a value of `NDIlib_frame_type_status_change` when this setting is known (or when it has changed). #### PTZ Control\n\nThere are standard API functions to execute the standard set of PTZ commands. This list is not designed to be exhaustive and may be expanded in the future. It is generally recommended that PTZ cameras provide a web interface to give access to the full set of capabilities of the camera and that the host application control the basic messages listed below. #### Zoom Level\n\n> `bool NDIlib_recv_ptz_zoom(NDIlib_recv_instance_t p_instance, const float zoom_value);`\n\nSet the camera zoom level. The zoom value ranges from 0. 0 to 1. 0. #### Zoom Speed\n\n> `bool NDIlib_recv_ptz_zoom_speed(NDIlib_recv_instance_t p_instance, const float zoom_speed);`\n\nControl the zoom level as a speed value. The zoom speed value is in the range [-1. 0, +1. 0] with zero indicating no motion. #### Pan and Tilt\n\n> `bool NDIlib_recv_ptz_pan_tilt_speed(NDIlib_recv_instance_t p_instance, const float pan_speed, const float tilt_speed);`\n\nThis will tell the camera to move with a specific speed toward a direction. The speed is specified in a range [-1. 0, 1. 0], with 0. 0 meaning no motion. > `bool NDIlib_recv_ptz_pan_tilt(NDIlib_recv_instance_t p_instance, const float pan_value, const float tilt_value);`\n\nThis will set the absolute values for pan and tilt. The range of these values is [-1. 0, +1. 0], with 0. 0 representing center. #### Presets\n\n> `bool NDIlib_recv_ptz_store_preset(NDIlib_recv_instance_t p_instance, const int preset_no);`\n\nStore the current camera position as a preset. The preset number is in the range 0 to 99. > `bool NDIlib_recv_ptz_recall_preset(NDIlib_recv_instance_t p_instance, const int preset_no, const float speed);`\n\nRecall a PTZ preset. The preset number is in the range 0 to 99. The speed value is in the range 0. 0 to 1. 0, and controls how fast it will move to the preset. #### Focus\n\nFocus on cameras can either be in auto-focus mode or in manual focus mode. The following are examples of these commands:\n\n> `bool NDIlib_recv_ptz_auto_focus(NDIlib_recv_instance_t p_instance);`\n> \n> `bool NDIlib_recv_ptz_focus(NDIlib_recv_instance_t p_instance, const float focus_value);`\n\nIf the mode is auto, then there are no other settings. If the mode is manual, then the value is the focus distance, specified in the range 0. 0 to 1. 0. If you wish to control the focus by speed instead of absolute value, you may do this as follows:\n\n> `bool NDIlib_recv_ptz_focus_speed(NDIlib_recv_instance_t p_instance, const float focus_speed);`\n\nThe focus speed is in the range -1. 0 to +1. 0, with 0. 0 indicating no change in focus value. **White Balance**\n\nWhite balance can be in a variety of modes, including the following:\n\n> `bool NDIlib_recv_ptz_white_balance_auto(NDIlib_recv_instance_t p_instance);`\n\nThis will place the camera in auto-white balance mode. > `bool NDIlib_recv_ptz_white_balance_indoor(NDIlib_recv_instance_t p_instance);`\n\nThis will place the camera in auto-white balance mode, but with a preference for indoor settings. > `bool NDIlib_recv_ptz_white_balance_outdoor(NDIlib_recv_instance_t p_instance);`\n\nThis will place the camera in auto-white balance mode, but with a preference for outdoor settings. > `bool NDIlib_recv_ptz_white_balance_manual(NDIlib_recv_instance_t p_instance, const float red, const float blue);`\n\nThis allows for manual white balancing, with the red and blue values in the range 0. 0 to 1. 0. > `bool NDIlib_recv_ptz_white_balance_oneshot(NDIlib_recv_instance_t p_instance);`\n\nThis allows you to set up the white balance automatically using the current center of the camera position. It will then store that value as the white-balance setting. **Exposure Control**\n\nExposure can either be automatic or manual. > `bool NDIlib_recv_ptz_exposure_auto(NDIlib_recv_instance_t p_instance);`\n\nThis will place the camera in auto-exposure mode. > `bool NDIlib_recv_ptz_exposure_manual_v2(NDIlib_recv_instance_t p_instance, const float iris, const float gain, const float shutter_speed);`\n\n### Receivers and Tally Messages\n\nVideo receivers can specify whether the source is visible on a video switcher’s program or preview row. This is communicated up-stream to the source’s sender, which then indicates its state (see the section on the sender SDK within this document). The sender takes its state and echoes it to all receivers as a metadata message of the form:\n\n> `<ndi_tally_echo on_program=\"true\" on_preview=\"false\"/>`\n\nThis message is very useful, allowing every receiver to ‘know’ whether its source is on program output. To illustrate, consider a sender named “My Source A” sending to two destinations, “Switcher” and “Multi-viewer”. When “Switcher” places “My Source A” on program out, a tally message is sent from “Switcher” to “My Source A”. Thus, the source ‘knows’ it is visible on program output. At this point, it will echo its tally state to “Multi-viewer” (and “Switcher”) so that the receiver is aware that “My Source A” is on program out. This functionality is used in the NDI tools Studio Monitor application to display an indicator when the source monitored has its tally state set. ### Frame Synchronization\n\nWhen using video, it is important to realize that different clocks are often used by different parts of the signal chain. Within NDI, the sender can send at the clock rate it wants, and the receiver will receive it at that rate. In many cases, however, the sender and receiver are extremely unlikely to share the exact same clock rate. Bear in mind that computer clocks rely on crystals which – while notionally rated for the same frequency – are seldom truly identical. For example, your sending computer might have an audio clock rated to operate at 48000 Hz. However, it might well actually run at 48001 Hz, or perhaps 47998 Hz. Similar variances also affect receivers. While the differences appear miniscule, they can accumulate to cause significant audio sync drift over time. A receiver may receive more samples than it plays back, or audible glitches can occur because too few audio samples are sent in a given time span. Naturally, the same problem affects video sources. It is very common to address these timing discrepancies by having a \"frame buffer\" and displaying the most recently received video frame. Unfortunately, the deviations in clock timing prevent this from being a perfect solution. Frequently, for example, the video will appear to ‘jitter’ when the sending and receiving clocks are almost aligned (which is actually the most common case). A \"time base corrector\" (TBC) or frame-synchronizer for the video clock provides another mechanism to handle these issues. This approach uses hysteresis to determine the best time to either drop or insert a video frame to achieve smooth video playback (audio should be dynamically sampled with a high-order resampling filter to adaptively track clocking differences). It’s quite difficult to develop something that is correct for all of the diverse scenarios that can arise, so the NDI SDK provides an implementation to help you develop real-time audio/video applications without assuming responsibility for the significant complexity involved. Another way to view what this component of the SDK does is to think of it as transforming ‘push’ sources (i. e. , NDI sources in which the data is pushed from the sender to the receiver) into ‘pull’ sources, wherein the host application pulls the data down-stream. The frame sync automatically tracks all clocks to achieve the best video and audio performance while doing so. In addition to time-base correction operations, NDI’s frame sync will also automatically detect and correct for timing jitter that might occur. On a multiviewer, you would have a frame-sync for every video source, then call all of them on each v-sync and redraw all sources at that time. **Audio playback through sound card**\n\n**Yes** – the clock should be synced with your sound card clock. **Video mixing of sources**\n\n**Yes** – all video input clocks need to be synced to your output video clock. You can take each of the video inputs and frame-synchronize them together. **Audio mixing**\n\n**Yes** – you want all input audio clocks to be brought into sync with your output audio clock. You would create a frame-synchronizer for each audio source and – when driving the output – call each one, asking for the correct number of samples and sample rate for your output. **Recording a single channel **\n\n**No** – you should record the signal in the raw form without any re-clocking. **Recording multiple channels**\n\n**Maybe** – If you want to sync some input channels to match a master clock so that they can be ISO-edited, you might want a frame-sync for all sources except one (allowing them all to be synchronized with a single channel). To create a frame synchronizer object, you will call the function below (that is based on an already instantiated NDI receiver from which it will get frames). Once this receiver has been bound to a frame sync, you should use it in order to recover video frames. You can continue to use the underlying receiver for other operations, such as tally, PTZ, metadata, etc. Remember, it remains your responsibility to destroy the receiver – even when a frame-sync is using it (you should always destroy the receiver after the framesync has been destroyed). > `NDIlib_framesync_instance_t NDIlib_framesync_create(NDIlib_recv_instance_t p_receiver);`\n\nThe frame-sync is destroyed with the corresponding call:\n\n> `void NDIlib_framesync_destroy(NDIlib_framesync_instance_t p_instance);`\n\nIn order to recover audio, the following function will pull audio samples from the frame-sync queue. This function will always return data immediately, inserting silence if no current audio data is present. You should call this at the rate that you want audio, and it will automatically use dynamic audio sampling to conform the incoming audio signal to the rate at which you are calling. Note that you have no obligation to ensure that your requested sample rate, channel count, and number of samples match the incoming signal and that all combinations of conversions are supported. Audio resampling is done with high-order audio filters. Timecode and per-frame metadata are inserted into the best possible audio samples. Also, if you specify the desired sample rate as zero, it will fill in the buffer (and audio data descriptor) with the original audio sample rate. If you specify the channel count as zero, it will fill in the buffer (and audio data descriptor) with the original audio channel count. The buffer returned is freed using the corresponding function:\n\ntime-basedThis function will pull video samples from the frame-sync queue. It will always immediately return a video sample by using time-based correction. You can specify the desired field type, which is then used to return the best possible frame. Note that:\n* Field-based frame sync means that the frame synchronizer attempts to match the fielded input phase with the frame requests to provide the most correct possible field ordering on output. * The same frame can be returned multiple times if duplication is needed to match the timing criteria. It is assumed that progressive video sources can **i)** correctly display either a field 0 or field 1,** ii) **that fielded sources can correctly display progressive sources, and **iii)** that the display of field 1 on a field 0 (or vice versa) should be avoided at all costs. If no video frame has ever been received, this will return `NDIlib_video_frame_v2_t` as an empty (all zero) structure. This allows you to determine that there has not yet been any video and act accordingly (for instance, you might want to display a constant frame output in a particular video format or black). The buffer returned is freed using the corresponding function:\n\nLast updated 4 months ago\n\nWas this helpful?\n\n2024 @ NDI Vizrt AB. * [Parameters][62]\n* [Receiver User Interfaces][63]\n* [Receiver PTZ Control][64]\n* [Receivers and Tally Messages][65]\n* [Frame Synchronization][66]\n\nWas this helpful?\n\nCopy\n\n`NDIlib_video_frame_v2_t video_frame;\nNDIlib_audio_frame_v3_t audio_frame; \nNDIlib_metadata_frame_t metadata_frame;\n\nswitch (NDIlib_recv_capture_v3(pRecv, &video_frame, &audio_frame, &metadata_frame, 1000)) \n{\n\n    // We received video. case NDIlib_frame_type_video:\n        // Process video here\n        // Free the video. NDIlib_recv_free_video_v2(pRecv, &video_frame); \n        break;\n\n    // We received audio. case NDIlib_frame_type_audio:\n        // Process audio here\n        // Free the audio. NDIlib_recv_free_audio_v3(pRecv, &audio_frame);\n        break;\n\n    // We received a metadata packet \n    case NDIlib_frame_type_metadata:\n        // Do what you want with the metadata message here. // Free the message \n        NDIlib_recv_free_metadata(pRecv, &metadata_frame); \n        break;\n\n    // No audio or video has been received in the time-period. case NDIlib_frame_type_none:\n        break;\n\n    // The device has changed status in some way (see notes below) \n    case NDIlib_frame_type_status_change:\n        break;\n}    `\n\nCopy\n\n`// Provide a metadata registration that allows people to know what we are. NDIlib_metadata_frame_t NDI_product_type;\nNDI_product_type. p_data =  \"<ndi_product long_name=\\\"NDILib Receive Example. \\\" \" \n                           \"             short_name=\\\"NDILib Receive\\\" \"\n                           \"             manufacturer=\\\"CoolCo, inc. \\\" \"\n                           \"             version=\\\"1. }`\n\nCopy\n\n`void NDIlib_framesync_capture_audio(\n    NDIlib_framesync_instance_t p_instance, // The frame sync instance \n    NDIlib_audio_frame_v2_t* p_audio_data, // The destination audio buffer \n    int sample_rate, // Your desired sample rate. 0 for “use source”. int no_channels, // Your desired channel count. 0 for “use source”. int no_samples); // The number of audio samples that you wish to get. `\n\nCopy\n\n`void NDIlib_framesync_free_audio(NDIlib_framesync_instance_t p_instance,        \n                                 NDIlib_audio_frame_v2_t* p_audio_data);`\n\nCopy\n\n`void NDIlib_framesync_capture_video(\n    NDIlib_framesync_instance_t p_instance, // The frame-sync instance \n    NDIlib_video_frame_v2_t* p_video_data, // The destination video frame \n    NDIlib_frame_format_type_e field_type); // The frame type that you prefer`\n\nCopy\n\n`void NDIlib_framesync_free_video(NDIlib_framesync_instance_t p_instance, \n                                 NDIlib_video_frame_v2_t* p_video_data);`\n\n[1]: /all\n[2]: https://docs. ndi. video/all/using-ndi/ndi-tools\n[3]: /all/developing-with-ndi/sdk\n[4]: /all/getting-started/white-paper\n[5]: /all\n[6]:
